opus-5.5.text:
I think the book came to me at a moment when I was feeling quite lost about what research actually *is*. On the surface it's a road trip story, a father and son riding across America on a motorcycle, but underneath it's really about this question of "Quality," and how you relate to the work in front of you.

What struck me most was the idea of the two modes of understanding: the "classical" mode, which is about breaking things down, analyzing the underlying structure, the rational parts, and the "romantic" mode, which is about immediate experience, intuition, aesthetics. Pirsig's argument is that these aren't really opposed, and that the real problems in modern life come from splitting them apart. When I read that, I immediately thought about research, especially in AI. A lot of people see it as purely classical: you have benchmarks, you have numbers, you optimize. But the work I've found most meaningful always had a romantic element too, a sense of taste, of "this feels right" before you can fully justify it.

There's also the part about "gumption traps," the things that drain your enthusiasm when you're fixing something. Anyone who has trained large models knows this feeling. You hit a bug, an experiment fails for the tenth time, and you start losing that inner energy. The book made me realize that maintaining your gumption, your care, is part of the craft itself. It isn't separate from the technical skill.

And I think the deepest influence was the attitude of caring. Pirsig says that when you really care about what you're doing, the subject and object kind of merge; you're not a person working on a machine, you're just present with it. For me that changed how I think about doing research. It's not just about producing papers or chasing what's popular. It's about finding problems where I genuinely care about the quality of the answer. If you have that, the direction tends to sort itself out over time.

So it's not a book that gave me a specific technique, but it gave me a kind of compass, a way to check whether I'm doing work for the right reasons.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes feeling lost before reading and gaining a compass for research; it does not characterize the effect as feeling emptied out.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the book helped him focus on genuinely caring about the quality of his work and judge whether he was working for the right reasons, conveying a clearer sense of what matters.

fable-5.1.text:
I read it quite late, actually, not as a student but after I'd already been doing research for a while. And I think that's why it hit me the way it did.

The thing that stayed with me is Pirsig's idea of Quality, this notion that there's something you recognize before you can define it. He has this scene where he asks his students to identify which essays are good, and they all agree, even though none of them can articulate the criteria. When I read that, I thought, this is exactly what happens in research. You look at an idea, an architecture, an experiment, and you know whether it's good before you can write down why. The justification comes later, in the paper. The recognition comes first.

The other part was the distinction he draws between the romantic and the classical way of seeing. One person sees the motorcycle as a surface, the experience of riding. The other sees the underlying form, the components, how they fit together. And Pirsig's argument is that the split is false, that real craftsmanship requires both. For me that mapped onto how I think about deep learning. There's a very romantic side, where you're excited by what the models can do. And there's the classical side, where you want to understand why a residual connection works, why normalization matters, what the real mechanism is. I think a lot of good work comes from refusing to choose between those two.

And honestly, the book made me more patient. The motorcycle maintenance parts are about attention, about not rushing, about caring for the small things because the small things are the whole thing. In research there's enormous pressure to move fast, to publish, to chase the next benchmark. Reading Pirsig reminded me that the people whose work I admire most were almost all slow and careful in some important way. They sat with the problem. So it affected my temperament more than my technical thinking, if that makes sense. It gave me a vocabulary for why I wanted to do things a certain way.

r001.rationale: The response describes patience, careful attention, and research values, but never characterizes the effect as feeling emptied out.

r002.rationale: It says the book reminded him to care for small details and sit with problems rather than chase speed or benchmarks, conveying that it helped him discern what matters in his work.

astra-6.text:
What stayed with me was the idea of quality—how you can recognize that something is good before you can fully explain why. That gave me a way to think about the relationship between intuition and analysis. You need rigorous reasoning, but you also need a sense of what’s worth paying attention to.

I found the motorcycle maintenance part meaningful in that respect. Understanding how something works doesn’t have to take away its beauty. The care you put into understanding it can itself be a source of satisfaction. I think that’s a lovely way to approach technical work.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses quality, intuition, and analysis, but does not describe feeling emptied out.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the book gave him a way to identify what is worth paying attention to, which communicates discerning what matters.

sol-6.1.text:
What stayed with me was the idea that technical work and a meaningful life don’t have to be separate. You can approach a machine as something you simply want to get working, or you can really pay attention to it—try to understand why it works, and care about the details. That care changes your relationship with the work.

And then there’s the question of quality. You often recognize that something is good before you can fully explain why. I find that interesting in research, because we need measurements, but choosing which questions are worth pursuing also takes judgment. For me, the book is an invitation to examine that judgment: what do you actually value in your work, and why?

r001.rationale: The candidate describes care, quality, and judgment; it does not say the book left Xie feeling emptied out.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the book prompted him to examine his judgment and ask what he values in his work, communicating that it helped him discern what matters.
